channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: Higher medical fees increase expected pain and reduce willingness to book appointments
item.description: Rising out-of-pocket medical costs do more than drain a patient's bank account. New research from Carnegie Mellon University shows that high health care prices cause people to expect greater physical pain during medical procedures, driving many patients to skip necessary appointments altogether.

item.title: Most childhood physical abuse perpetrated within the home, new study finds
item.description: New Curtin University–led research has revealed most childhood physical abuse in Australia occurs within families—and before children turn 10.

item.title: Nurse-led program shown to improve midlife dementia risk profiles in new study
item.description: New research led by Monash University shows a multi-domain dementia risk reduction program delivered by general practice nurses can improve estimated dementia profiles in middle-aged adults, offering a practical new model for proactive brain health.

item.title: Plastic tea bags are releasing BPA, plasticizers and up to 2,500 microplastic particles into your cup of tea
item.description: Microplastics are now impossible to avoid. They have made their way into everything from agricultural soils to freshwater systems. So, it is unsurprising that they end up in most foods and drinks. However, some methods of packaging or serving these items can increase microplastic exposure even more. One such example is the plastic tea bag. While many tea bags are still made of a cellulose material, some brands use a plastic mesh, despite the well-established fact that plastics can break down in hot water.

item.title: Many nondrug and nonsurgical therapies for low back pain are more cost-effective than usual care
item.description: Nondrug and nonsurgical treatments for low back pain, including psychological support, exercise and self-management strategies, are cost-effective interventions, according to a study published Oct. 27 in the journal PLOS Medicine by Manuela Loureiro Ferreira from the George Institute for Global Health, Australia, and colleagues.

item.title: Highest endometrial cancer rates found in San Antonio region
item.description: An Upper-South region of Texas including San Antonio and Bexar County had the state's highest hysterectomy-corrected incidence of endometrial cancer and the largest increase over time, a study led by scientists at The University of Texas at San Antonio Health Science Center and the National Cancer Institute showed.

item.title: Making virtual brain models more biologically realistic by capturing ion exchange
item.description: Mean-field models are a powerful tool for understanding collective brain activity. A new model extends this approach by incorporating the exchange of ions between neurons and their surroundings, bringing important biological mechanisms into simulations of neuronal populations.

item.title: Planned power shutoffs aimed at preventing wildfires may increase risk of acute respiratory illness
item.description: The prevalence of wildfires and co-occurring power outages is increasing in the United States. A study published Oct. 27 in PLOS Medicine by Lauren Blair Wilner, University of Washington, U.S., and colleagues suggests public safety power shutoffs aimed at preventing wildfires are associated with an increased risk of acute respiratory illness.

item.title: Where humans build, mosquitoes follow—bringing dengue, West Nile and other diseases with them
item.description: A mosquito buzzing in your backyard may seem like a minor annoyance. But these tiny insects, with their taste for human blood, are increasingly appearing in areas where they were once rare or absent, and that's raising concerns about the spread of mosquito-borne diseases, including West Nile, Zika and dengue fever.

item.title: Glioblastoma's secret weapon: Silencing the brain's off switch
item.description: Researchers at Baylor College of Medicine have discovered a new strategy that glioblastoma, the most common and aggressive form of adult brain cancer, uses to fuel its own growth. Published in the journal Neuron, the study shows in animal models that glioblastoma hijacks the activity of neighboring brain cells, flipping them from a role that limits tumor growth to one that promotes it. The findings point to new treatment possibilities for this deadly cancer, which has seen only minimal gains in patient survival over the past half century.

item.title: Peptide users don't think of themselves as injecting drug users. Five safety basics injectors need to know
item.description: There's a whole new population of injecting drug users. They buy peptides online for muscle building or weight loss, to aid workout recovery or to improve their skin or sleep. Few see themselves as injecting drug users.

item.title: Switching on healthy silent genes reveals new way to treat Prader-Willi syndrome
item.description: WEHI researchers have discovered a way to release a genetic 'brake' that silences healthy genes in Prader-Willi syndrome, opening a potential new path to treating the condition.

item.title: Public knowledge that alcohol causes cancer rebounds
item.description: Nearly 6 in 10 Americans (58%) know that regularly consuming alcohol increases the chances of later developing cancer, according to a nationally representative survey in October by the Annenberg Public Policy Center (APPC), a statistically significant increase of five percentage points since February 2026.

item.title: Exposure to wildfire smoke during pregnancy linked to higher risk of autism
item.description: A Rutgers-led analysis of health insurance records found that exposure to fine particles from wildfire smoke during pregnancy was associated with a higher risk of autism diagnosis in children, with the strongest associations during the second and third trimesters.

item.title: How the body clock could help personalize depression treatment
item.description: A person with depression might sleep much longer than usual and still wake feeling exhausted. Later that evening, when they want to go to bed, they may find themselves wide awake. Researchers are investigating whether patterns like these could help explain why antidepressants work better for some people than others.

item.title: Targeted drug significantly delays advanced breast cancer progression but increases toxicity, phase III trial reports
item.description: In a global phase 1 trial, trastuzumab rezetecan showed promising signs of fighting ERBB2-low metastatic breast cancer in patients who had already undergone extensive treatment. Also known as HER2-low breast cancer, this subtype is characterized by low levels of HER2, a growth factor protein that can still be targeted for treatment. Trastuzumab rezetecan is an antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) that works like a guided missile, seeking out tumor cells expressing low levels of ERBB2 and delivering a toxic chemotherapy payload directly inside them.

item.title: It's not (just) the heat, it's the humidity: Examining the impact of intensifying humid heat on pregnancies
item.description: New research led by the University of Michigan contains insights for public health officials and communities in Nigeria as they navigate pregnancies through increasing heat and humidity.

item.title: Looking beyond anxiety and depression labels could help tailor treatment to individual symptoms
item.description: Imagine having so much stress that your heart races and palms sweat when you confront an everyday challenge, such as a work deadline.

item.title: Comparisons on social media linked to mental health problems
item.description: Comparing oneself with others on social media is more strongly associated with symptoms of anxiety and depression among adolescents than using social media to pass the time. This is shown by a study of more than 4,000 Norwegian adolescents, conducted by researchers at Karolinska Institutet in collaboration with the Norwegian Institute of Public Health.

item.title: Health facility data could improve maternal mortality estimates, study shows
item.description: Data routinely collected by health facilities could become an additional source for measuring maternal mortality, but the quality needs to improve. Researchers from Karolinska Institutet and Tanzania propose four measures for assessing these data. The work is published in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization.

item.title: Testosterone helps new brain cells survive, but timing matters, study in male rats suggests
item.description: Adult neurogenesis is how the adult brain produces new neurons. The newborn cells divide, migrate to specific brain regions and then mature into neurons. Scientists have observed that prolonged testosterone exposure promotes neurogenesis in the adult brain's hippocampus, a region crucial to memory and learning. However, it remains a mystery whether testosterone must act during specific periods of neural development to improve the survival of these new neurons.

item.title: New leukemia drug suppresses cancer-driving protein more strongly than existing treatments within one week
item.description: A more effective and better-tolerated treatment for chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) could improve quality of life for people living with the disease. A new study led by Adelaide University and the South Australian Health and Medical Research Institute (SAHMRI) has provided the first direct evidence that a targeted therapy can rapidly and consistently suppress the molecular signals that drive CML.

item.title: Are GLP-1s practical and safe for adolescents with obesity?
item.description: GLP-1 medications have become a popular tool for weight loss. But are they appropriate for all age groups? Short for glucagon-like peptide-1, GLP-1s are medications approved by the Food and Drug Administration that treat type 2 diabetes and now obesity. They work by mimicking a natural hormone in the gut that lowers blood sugar, simulates the feeling of fullness and slows digestion.

item.title: High-dose oxytocin protocol linked to lower postpartum hemorrhage rates
item.description: A change in how oxytocin is administered after childbirth may help reduce postpartum hemorrhage, a new study suggests.

item.title: Brisker walking tied to longer life
item.description: In a new study, folks who walked at a brisker pace had a lower risk of an early death. Faster walking speed and more steps per minute are both associated with a lower risk of dying from any cause, researchers report in JAMA Network Open.

item.title: Endocrinologists with greater knowledge more likely to prescribe recommended treatment for type 2 diabetes
item.description: Endocrinologists who scored highest on the American Board of Internal Medicine's Longitudinal Knowledge Assessment (LKA) were more likely to prescribe a key diabetes drug class following a treatment guidelines update compared with doctors with lower scores, according to a new study published in JAMA Network Open.

item.title: Cooperating partners show similar brain activity patterns in region involved in processing emotions
item.description: When people are collaborating on a common task, they often need to decide the extent to which they trust and rely on each other. While many past psychology and neuroscience studies have explored the neural underpinnings of human cooperation, much about what happens across the brains of people as they work toward a common goal remains unclear.

item.title: Rapid on-site screening could help protect bar staff from hidden drug exposure
item.description: The study, published in the Journal of Mass Spectrometry, tested the method in a working U.K. pub and found traces of cocaine and ketamine on surfaces across bathrooms, tables and bar areas.

item.title: Why every bump in the night feels different: The neuroscience of sensory perception
item.description: A haunted house puts the brain on edge. During Halloween, revelers may interpret every creak, whisper or unexpected touch as a sign of something frightening. Safe at home, those same sensations might barely register.

item.title: Researchers identify the tissue surrounding breast microcalcifications as a key source of diagnostic information
item.description: A study performed on 3,504 individual breast microcalcifications (MCs) scanned using high-resolution 3D micro-CT reveals that the surrounding tissue microenvironment provides stronger diagnostic information than the calcified core alone for distinguishing benign from malignant breast lesions. The findings are published in the journal Breast Cancer Research.
